passage: Jyoti sat on the roof of her new house in a small town near Sangli, watching buffaloes cross the dusty road. She missed the noisy lanes of Mumbai and the way Rehana used to save half her tiffin for her. Her throat tightened. That evening she borrowed her aunt's phone and called Rehana, who laughed and told her all about the school play. Afterwards Jyoti wrote a long letter and drew the buffaloes in the margin. The next day a girl named Sunita from the next lane peeped over the wall and asked what she was drawing. Jyoti hesitated, then held up the page. She still missed Mumbai, but she let Sunita sit on the wall beside her.

qa.q: What did Jyoti draw in the margin of her letter?
What was Jyoti feeling on the roof, and what does it show?
qa.a: Jyoti felt homesick and sad, missing the noisy lanes of Mumbai and Rehana; her throat tightened, which shows how much she cared for them.

qa.q: How can Jyoti keep her old friendship while making room for new ones?
qa.a: Keep calling and writing to Rehana, and let Sunita sit beside her.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel getting the call and the letter?
qa.a: Rehana laughed on the call and shared news, so Rehana is probably glad that Jyoti keeps in touch, and may miss Jyoti too.

grounding: A child misses her old friend and city, shows it by calling and writing, and also opens a small space for a new friend.

passage:
'Rehana! Can you see me? The screen's frozen.'
'Now I can. Arohi, you cut your hair!'
'Mumbai is so humid. It kept sticking to my neck.' Arohi laughed, then her voice went thin. 'I miss our terrace. I miss the chaat uncle. I miss you so much, it's silly.'
'It's not silly. We all went quiet at practice when Coach read out your name.'
'Really?'
'Really. Did you make any friends there?'
Arohi picked at the blanket. 'A girl called Nisha asked me to join the dance club. I said no. It felt like cheating on you all.'
'Cheating? Arohi, go! Then you can teach me the steps on Sunday's call.'
Arohi was quiet. 'Okay. Sunday call, same time?'
'Same time. Every Sunday.'

qa.q: Which club did Nisha invite Arohi to join?
Why did Arohi say no to the dance club?
qa.a: She missed her old friends so much that joining felt like cheating on them; she felt sad and a little guilty.

qa.q: What helps Arohi keep old friends and make room for new ones?
qa.a: Weekly Sunday calls with Rehana, and saying yes to the dance club so she can share the steps.

qa.q: How does Rehana see Arohi making new friends?
qa.a: As a good thing, not a betrayal; Rehana urges Arohi to go and share the steps 🤍

grounding: A girl who has moved city tells an old friend how much she misses home, and is encouraged to stay in touch and make new friends too.

passage: When we moved from Lucknow to Hyderabad last year, I refused to unpack my boxes for a month. My name is Nazia, and I was sure that if I kept them taped, we might somehow go back. I missed the azaan from our old mosque, the kebab smoke in the lane, and most of all Yusuf, who lived two doors down and taught me to fly kites. I wrote him long letters with pressed flowers inside. Then one letter from him said he had joined a kite club and made a friend called Ravi. My stomach dropped, and then something loosened. If Yusuf could keep me and still make room for Ravi, maybe I could do the same. That evening, I unpacked my first box.

qa.q: Who taught Nazia to fly kites?
qa.a: Yusuf, who lived two doors down.

qa.q: Why did Nazia keep the boxes taped?
qa.a: Nazia felt so homesick for Lucknow that unpacking felt like giving up hope of going back.

qa.q: What helped Nazia stop living only in the past?
qa.a: Seeing Yusuf keep their friendship while making a new friend, which showed there was room for both; then Nazia unpacked the first box.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel reading Nazia's long letters?
qa.a: Missed and cared for, since they came with pressed flowers; they show the friendship still matters.

grounding: A child who moved city misses an old friend deeply, writes to him, and slowly makes room for a new life.
